bibl.title: Measuring consciousness in severely damaged brains

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: In addition, functional neuroimaging paradigms are now available to help assess consciousness levels in this challenging patient population.

span.label: disorders of consciousness
span.quote: Significant advances have been made in the behavioral assessment and clinical management of disorders of consciousness (DOC).

span.label: review
span.quote: The promise of such theoretically based markers is illustrated by recent findings that used a perturbational approach to assess the levels of consciousness.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Consciousness arises from a system's capacity to integrate information, so that networks supporting it must strike an optimal balance between functional integration and differentiation
span.quote: In the case of the brain, the theory predicts that consciousness-supporting networks should present an optimal balance between functional integration and differentiation (Boly et al. 2009).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Loss of consciousness occurs through a breakdown of cortical effective connectivity, so that a local perturbation can no longer propagate as a widespread differentiated causal interaction
span.quote: During non–rapid eye movement sleep (NREM), under general anesthesia (e.g., midazolam), and in VS/UWS patients, TMS typically triggers a stereotypical slow wave that stays local, which indicates a breakdown of effective connectivity (Ferrarelli et al. 2010, Massimini et al. 2005, Rosanova et al. 2012).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Preserved cortical backward (top-down) connections generate the larger long-latency evoked components seen in MCS relative to VS/UWS
span.quote: The higher amplitude of long latency components in MCS patients as compared with VS/UWS patients could be linked to preserved function in cerebral backward connections (Figure 2f ) (Boly et al. 2011).

span.label: The assessment is gated by behaviour, so absence of response is not proof of absence of consciousness.
span.note: what this limits: any bedside diagnosis of unawareness: the authors state the assessment is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness and that absence of observed purposeful behaviors cannot be taken as definitive proof of the absence of consciousness
span.quote: bedside assessment of consciousness is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness. It is now increasingly more recognized that the absence of observed purposeful behaviors at the bedside cannot be taken as definitive proof of the absence of consciousness

span.label: The misdiagnosis rate is given together with the assessment method that produces it.
span.note: what this limits: any quoted misdiagnosis rate for unawareness: up to 40% applies when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales

span.label: A named patient group is misdiagnosed despite preserved awareness.
span.note: what this limits: any diagnosis of a disorder of consciousness: locked-in syndrome patients can be misdiagnosed as DOC despite preserved awareness, because of complete paralysis of voluntary muscles except vertical eye movements
span.quote: Finally, locked-in syndrome (LIS) patients can be misdiagnosed as DOC despite preserved awareness because of a complete paralysis of voluntary muscles, except vertical eye movements

span.label: The neuroimaging paradigm's validity rests on a control study the authors say is still needed.
span.note: what this limits: any use of an active-task neuroimaging paradigm as evidence of willful response: the authors state validation studies should be performed to ensure passive listening cannot elicit a similar brain activity pattern
span.quote: Thus, validation studies should be performed to ensure that the passive listening of the instruction to perform a task cannot elicit a brain activity pattern similar to the one from a voluntary response

span.label: the normalized Lempel-Ziv complexity measure, originally defined for finite symbol sequences, is computed on TMS-evoked EEG spatiotemporal response maps to yield the perturbational complexity index
span.quote: PCI estimates both the information content and the integration of brain activations through the computation of the normalized Lempel-Ziv complexity (Lempel & Ziv 1976) of the significant EEG spatiotemporal responses to TMS.

span.label: a separate experiment run on the same task
span.quote: In a separate experiment, this task was controlled for the absence of reflexive activation and, thus, for its specificity to detect only conscious responses (Naci et al. 2013).

span.label: comparing active against passive conditions, and runs attending to the patient's own name against runs attending to another name
span.quote: The search for a difference between active and passive conditions as well as between runs with attention to the patient’s own name and runs with attention to another name offers a control for both the presence of nonreflexive responses and for specificity.

span.label: instructing subjects NOT to perform the task and recording what happens
span.quote: Here again a control experiment shows no response when the subjects are instructed not to do the task.

span.label: behavioral responsiveness
span.quote: bedside assessment of consciousness is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness. It is now increasingly more recognized that the absence of observed purposeful behaviors at the bedside cannot be taken as definitive proof of the absence of consciousness

span.label: purposeful behaviors
span.quote: bedside assessment of consciousness is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness. It is now increasingly more recognized that the absence of observed purposeful behaviors at the bedside cannot be taken as definitive proof of the absence of consciousness

span.label: Misdiagnosis of unawareness
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales

span.label: clinical consensus
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales

span.label: locked-in syndrome
span.quote: Finally, locked-in syndrome (LIS) patients can be misdiagnosed as DOC despite preserved awareness because of a complete paralysis of voluntary muscles, except vertical eye movements

span.label: bedside consciousness - WHAT THE PATIENT CAN SHOW, NOT WHAT THEY HAVE: the assessment is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness, and the same reading is returned by a patient who is unconscious and by one who is conscious and unable to demonstrate it, which the review states cannot be treated as proof either way
span.quote: bedside assessment of consciousness is intrinsically gated by behavioral responsiveness. It is now increasingly more recognized that the absence of observed purposeful behaviors at the bedside cannot be taken as definitive proof of the absence of consciousness

span.label: the 40% misdiagnosis rate - CONDITIONAL ON THE INSTRUMENT: it applies to diagnosis based solely on clinical consensus without appropriate behavioral scales, so the number measures a practice rather than a difficulty, and the practice is nameable and fixable
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales

span.label: the active-task paradigm - VALID ONLY IF A CONTROL HOLDS THAT HAS NOT BEEN RUN: its status as evidence of willful response depends on passive listening not producing a similar pattern, and the authors say validation studies should be performed to establish that
span.quote: Thus, validation studies should be performed to ensure that the passive listening of the instruction to perform a task cannot elicit a brain activity pattern similar to the one from a voluntary response

span.label: qualifies → Ferreira (2007), Manning (2012)
span.note: differs in: WHO IS APPLYING THE CATEGORY. The law is stated as turning on the label - 'the right of the medical team TO WITHDRAW artificial nutrition and hydration from patients in VS/UWS, BUT NOT THOSE IN MCS' - and then: 'Opinions on these end-of-life decisions VARY, HOWEVER, depending NOT ONLY ON THE DIAGNOSIS of the patient, BUT ALSO ON THE PROFESSION AND THE CULTURAL BACKGROUND OF THE CLINICIANS'. So the same category, on the same patient, does not determine the same decision
span.quote: Legal precedence in several countries has established the right of the medical team to withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration from patients in VS/UWS, but not those in MCS (Ferreira 2007, Manning 2012). Opinions on these end-of-life decisions vary, however, depending not only on the diagnosis of the patient, but also on the profession and the cultural background of the clinicians (Demertzi et al. 2011).

span.label: contradicts → the assumption that locked-in patients have poor quality of life
span.note: differs in: WHO IS ASKED. The quality-of-life question 'is DIFFICULT TO ADDRESS IN THE ABSENCE OF COMMUNICATION with the patient' - and where communication IS possible the answer inverts: 'it is STRIKING to note, however, that MOST LIS PATIENTS REPORT SUBJECTIVE NEAR-TO-NORMAL QUALITY OF LIFE'. The inference drawn from outside about a state is contradicted by the only group in that state who can answer
span.quote: Another ethical concern is the quality of life in chronic DOC patients. This question is difficult to address in the absence of communication with the patient. In this context, it is striking to note, however, that most LIS patients report subjective near-to-normal quality of life (Bruno et al. 2011a).

span.label: builds-on → Schnakers et al. (2009)
span.note: differs in: WHICH INSTRUMENT PRODUCED THE DIAGNOSIS. The 40% figure is not a property of the patients: misdiagnosis is that frequent 'WHEN DIAGNOSIS IS BASED SOLELY ON CLINICAL CONSENSUS, WITHOUT USE OF APPROPRIATE BEHAVIORAL SCALES', and the review names the scale that does better in the next sentence. Quoted without its condition, the number describes the population rather than the procedure
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales (Schnakers et al. 2009). The most sensitive scale to differentiate MCS from VS/UWS is, to date, the revised version of the Coma Recovery Scale (CRS-R) (Giacino et al. 2004, Seel et al. 2010).

span.label: clinical consensus —causes→ Misdiagnosis of unawareness
span.note: holds when: when diagnosis rests on clinical consensus alone, without appropriate behavioral scales · direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales

span.label: Unawareness is misdiagnosed in up to 40% of cases when clinicians rely on consensus impression instead of a standardised behavioural scale.
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales (Schnakers et al. 2009).

span.label: Only about one in five patients with disorders of consciousness produces a positive response on active command-following neuroimaging paradigms.
span.quote: Recent cohort studies have indeed shown that only a minority, about 20%, of DOC patients can positively respond to this approach (Monti et al. 2010, Stender et al. 2014).

span.label: A negative result on an active paradigm is uninterpretable as evidence of unconsciousness, because aphasia, apraxia, fluctuating vigilance or unwillingness can all produce it.
span.quote: Thus, negative findings in the active paradigm can never exclude the possibility that the patient has retained awareness.

span.label: The perturbational complexity index separates conscious from unconscious states across subjects and conditions, staying above 0.31 in wakefulness, MCS, EMCS, LIS and REM sleep and below 0.31 in NREM sleep, vegetative state and anaesthesia.
span.quote: According to our current results, PCI is remarkably reliable to differentiate consciousness from unconsciousness within and across subjects and conditions: It is always high (i.e., above 0.31) in healthy awake subjects, in MCS, EMCS and LIS patients, as well as during REM sleep, but is invariably low (i.e., below 0.31) during NREM sleep, in patients in VS/UWS and under anesthesia-induced unconsciousness (using midazolam, propofol, or xenon) (Figure 5).

span.label: No conventional neuroimaging technique on its own is adequate to diagnose consciousness in a brain-damaged patient.
span.quote: Table 2 illustrates that, to date, none of the classical neuroimaging techniques mentioned above are sufficient to diagnose consciousness.

span.label: Preserved PET metabolism cannot serve as proof of consciousness, since metabolism can be normal or raised during epileptic seizures in which the subject is unconscious.
span.quote: And we know that during epileptic seizures, PET metabolism can be normal, or even increased, even though subjects are unconscious (Engel et al. 1982).

span.label: TMS delivered during NREM sleep, midazolam anaesthesia and vegetative state elicits only a local stereotypical slow wave, indicating a breakdown of effective connectivity, whereas conscious states give widespread differentiated responses.
span.quote: During non–rapid eye movement sleep (NREM), under general anesthesia (e.g., midazolam), and in VS/UWS patients, TMS typically triggers a stereotypical slow wave that stays local, which indicates a breakdown of effective connectivity (Ferrarelli et al. 2010, Massimini et al. 2005, Rosanova et al. 2012).

span.label: Neuroimaging and electrophysiology reliably separate MCS from VS/UWS at the group level, but single-subject interpretation of the same measures is often not possible.
span.quote: Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have identified consistent group differences in brain activity patterns in MCS patients as compared with VS/UWS patients.

span.label: Roughly 20% of patients diagnosed as vegetative show an atypical brain activity pattern, so outliers are expected in any group study.
span.quote: It is indeed common that about 20% of patients in VS/UWS present an atypical brain activity pattern.

span.label: The contents of consciousness in MCS remain inaccessible because these patients cannot give the reports on which content assessment normally depends.
span.quote: In MCS patients, no report can be obtained because no accurate communication is possible.

span.label: vegetative state / unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS)
span.quote: Vegetative state (VS)/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS): patients who are aroused but not aware of themselves and their surroundings

span.label: minimally conscious state (MCS)
span.quote: Minimally conscious state (MCS): patients who are aroused and show fluctuating signs of awareness without being able to functionally communicate

span.label: disorders of consciousness (DOC)
span.quote: Disorders of consciousness (DOC): refers to patients with severe acquired brain injuries in an altered state of consciousness; includes coma, VS/UWS, and MCS

span.label: locked-in syndrome (LIS)
span.quote: Locked-in syndrome (LIS): patients who are aroused and aware but who cannot move except to make eye movements

span.label: active paradigm
span.quote: Active paradigm: procedure that requires the subject to perform a specific task on request

span.label: passive paradigm
span.quote: Passive paradigm: procedure without any specific instruction where the subject does not do anything in particular

span.label: Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R)
span.quote: Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R): behavioral scale developed to assess the levels of consciousness in patients recovering from coma, and especially to differentiate conscious from unconscious patients

span.label: default mode network (DMN)
span.quote: Default mode network (DMN): a network of brain regions that are active when the awake subject is at rest

span.label: coma
span.quote: Coma is a transient state characterized by a complete absence of wakefulness and awareness (Plum & Posner 1983).

span.label: perturbational complexity index (PCI)
span.quote: We recently designed a new empirical measure known as the perturbational complexity index (PCI) to quantify in one number the difference in TMS-EEG responses present between states of consciousness and states of unconsciousness (Casali et al. 2013).

span.label: mismatch negativity (MMN)
span.quote: The mismatch negativity (MMN), an early negative waveform elicited by a deviant tone in a repetitive series, has been one of the most widely studied EEG components in patients with DOC.

span.label: transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
span.quote: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): technique that allows investigators to stimulate the brain noninvasively, which induces neuronal depolarization and discharge of action potentials

span.label: positron emission tomography (PET)
span.quote: Positron emission tomography (PET): invasive neuroimaging technique that measures brain metabolism energy turnover

span.label: up to 40% — rate of misdiagnosed unawareness when standardised behavioural scales are not used
span.quote: Misdiagnosis of unawareness is very frequent (up to 40%) when diagnosis is based solely on clinical consensus, without use of appropriate behavioral scales (Schnakers et al. 2009).

span.label: about 20% — share of DOC patients who respond positively to active command-following paradigms
span.quote: Recent cohort studies have indeed shown that only a minority, about 20%, of DOC patients can positively respond to this approach (Monti et al. 2010, Stender et al. 2014).

span.label: 0.31 — PCI threshold separating conscious from unconscious states
span.quote: According to our current results, PCI is remarkably reliable to differentiate consciousness from unconsciousness within and across subjects and conditions: It is always high (i.e., above 0.31) in healthy awake subjects, in MCS, EMCS and LIS patients, as well as during REM sleep, but is invariably low (i.e., below 0.31) during NREM sleep, in patients in VS/UWS and under anesthesia-induced unconsciousness (using midazolam, propofol, or xenon) (Figure 5).

span.label: 0.44 and 0.67 / 0.12 and 0.31 — observed PCI ranges in wakefulness versus in NREM sleep and anaesthesia
span.quote: PCI calculated during wakefulness ranges between 0.44 and 0.67, whereas PCI calculated during unconsciousness [i.e., non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and midazolam, xenon, or propofol anesthesia] ranges between 0.12 and 0.31.

span.label: about 20% — share of behaviourally vegetative patients showing an atypical brain activity pattern
span.quote: It is indeed common that about 20% of patients in VS/UWS present an atypical brain activity pattern.

span.label: 30 s — duration of each imagery block alternated with rest in the tennis imagery fMRI paradigm
span.quote: In this fMRI paradigm, patients are instructed to repetitively alternate 30 s of motor imagery (i.e., playing tennis) or spatial navigation mental imagery (i.e., walking in your house) with 30 s of rest.

span.label: 7 / 3 of 10 — authors' experience of how many bedside-diagnosed VS/UWS patients show the classical hypometabolic PET pattern versus preserved metabolism
span.quote: In our experience, out of these 10 patients, 7 will show a classical frontoparietal hypometabolic PET pattern, and 3 will have preserved metabolism of PET.

span.label: >6 — CRS-R total score on admission that acts as a favourable prognostic factor
span.quote: Other prognostic factors are the CRS-R total score on admission (i.e., >6) (Estraneo et al. 2013), a young age (Howell et al. 2013), a traumatic etiology (Multi-Society Task Force on PVS 1994b), an early time since onset (Whyte et al. 2009), the presence of pupillary light reflexes (Fischer et al. 2006), the absence of medical complications (Whyte et al. 2013), and specialized early treatment (Seel et al. 2013).

span.label: minimum 5 times — number of repeated CRS-R assessments the authors recommend before a final diagnosis
span.quote: Repeat assessments combining morning and afternoon evaluations, minimum 5 times total for a final
